content: The evidence supporting the public health impact of laws and policies is inherently complex. This complexity arises from the fact that such evidence does not easily lend itself to randomized controlled trials or comparative observational studies. Furthermore, synthesizing this evidence using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) approach is not straightforward. As a result, a pragmatic approach was adopted to address these challenges. The Evidence Synthesis Teams (ESTs) were responsible for planning and conducting systematic reviews and preparing the GRADE Evidence-to-Decision (EtD) frameworks. These frameworks included evidence summaries, evidence profiles or tables, and EtD tables. The ESTs were composed of researchers from the World Health Organization (WHO), consultants, fellows, and external collaborating research groups. For the clinical services domain, the EST included members from the Cochrane Fertility Regulation (CFR) Group, family planning fellows (WHO staff or interns), and the technical officer responsible for the guideline's Steering Group. For the service delivery domain, the EST included staff from Cochrane Response, family planning fellows (current and former WHO staff), and the responsible technical officer from the Steering Group. Cochrane Response, a consultancy service operated by the Cochrane Collaboration, provided tailored and responsive evidence services, including accessible review formats. The CFR Group and Cochrane Response updated their systematic reviews to provide the evidence base for many of the recommendations in the clinical services and service delivery domains. For the law and policy domain, the EST included WHO consultants and external teams from two centers: the Policy Surveillance Program at the Center for Public Health Law Research (CPHLR) at Temple University, USA, and the Birmingham Law School at the University of Birmingham, UK. The CPHLR team developed conceptual frameworks, legal mappings of interventions, and systems, and identified data for empirical assessments of laws and policies. The Birmingham team contributed expertise in health law and policy, human rights, comparative law, and global legal studies, conducting systematic reviews to support the law and policy recommendations. The Evidence and Recommendation Review Groups (ERRGs) and the Guideline Development Group (GDG) were integral to the guideline development process. Instead of forming a single GDG at the outset, three separate ERRGs were established for the clinical services, service delivery, and law and policy domains. Each ERRG had 6–13 members representing all regions and a range of expertise, including a youth representative from the International Youth Alliance for Family Planning (IYAFP). These members were identified and invited by the WHO Steering Group, along with human rights advisors who ensured the inclusion of relevant human rights considerations during recommendation formulation. The ERRGs reviewed evidence, formulated draft recommendations, and reached consensus during a series of online meetings held between March 2020 and March 2021. Background documents, including EtD frameworks and draft recommendations, were shared with ERRG members before each meeting. Additional consultations were conducted via email, Skype, Microsoft Teams, GoToMeeting, and Zoom as needed. In early 2021, representatives from each ERRG were invited to join the GDG for a final meeting in April 2021. During this meeting, draft recommendations from all three ERRGs were reviewed and finalized. The GDG, comprising 18 members (14 female, 4 male) from all six WHO regions, included a youth representative from IYAFP. The GDG reviewed the evidence and draft recommendations to reach consensus on the certainty of the evidence and the strength and direction of the recommendations. Following the meeting, members reviewed the revised guideline document, which incorporated decisions made during the GDG meeting. The External Review Group (ERG) was composed of nine technical experts and stakeholders with thematic expertise relevant to the recommendations. These members were identified by the WHO Steering Group in consultation with the GDG. The ERG ensured geographic representation and the absence of significant conflicts of interest. The ERG reviewed the draft guideline document, providing input on accuracy, clarity, implementation considerations, and presentation. While the ERG did not alter the finalized recommendations, their feedback improved the document's clarity and readability. All comments were collated by the responsible technical officer and reviewed by the WHO Steering Group. Observers and external partners were invited to the GDG meeting in April 2021, in line with the WHO handbook for guideline development. These observers, including representatives from professional organizations and United Nations agencies, had no role in determining the recommendations. Invited organizations included the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RCOG), the International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO), the International Confederation of Midwives (ICM), and the International Council of Nurses (ICN). Additionally, implementing partner organizations such as Ipas, the International Planned Parenthood Federation (IPPF), MSI Reproductive Choices, Pathfinder, and Population Services International (PSI) were invited to review the draft guideline before submission to the Guidelines Review Committee (GRC). All participants, including consultants and collaborators, were required to declare any competing interests in writing before participating in the guideline development or evidence review process. This was done through the electronic submission of a signed WHO Declaration of Interests (DOI) form and a copy of their curriculum vitae. Internet searches were conducted to identify any undisclosed potential conflicts of interest. The responsible technical officer assessed the DOI forms and CVs in consultation with the Director of the SRH Department and the WHO Steering Group to determine the existence and severity of any conflicts of interest. A management plan was agreed upon for any identified conflicts. One conflict arose for an ERRG member during the guideline development process, and this individual did not attend subsequent meetings. No other significant conflicts of interest were identified. All ERRG, GDG, and ERG members were instructed to notify the responsible technical officer of any changes in relevant interests during their participation. At the start of each meeting, participants had the opportunity to verbally confirm, amend, or append their declared interests. They could also do so in writing before submitting comments on draft versions of the guideline. Additionally, all members of the ERRGs, GDG, ERG, ESTs, and guideline methodologists signed confidentiality agreements related to the guideline development process and outcomes. The responsible technical officer securely stored all DOI forms and CVs to maintain confidentiality. The scope of the guidance was defined through an online survey conducted in September 2018 to identify areas requiring updates or new additions to the WHO guidance on safe abortion. The survey also sought suggestions for making the guidelines more user-friendly. It was distributed within various sexual and reproductive health networks and received 122 responses. Scoping meetings for the clinical services, service delivery, and law and policy domains were held between November 2018 and June 2019 to determine key topic areas and formulate key questions in the PICO format (Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcomes). These questions were reviewed, modified, and finalized through follow-up communications between the WHO Steering Group and ERRG members. The PICO questions for each domain were used to guide systematic reviews and evidence retrieval. Sources for evidence included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), non-randomized controlled trials, controlled before-and-after studies, interrupted time series, and cohort studies. The systematic reviews conducted for the guideline development are detailed in Annex 7, along with supplementary materials and search strategies.
